analysis.one_liner: Lets Congress void batches of a president's last-minute regulations in a single vote.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 240–179 on November 17, 2016, but the Senate never voted, and it died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill changes the Congressional Review Act, the law that lets Congress cancel new federal regulations. Today Congress must vote on each regulation separately; the bill would let lawmakers bundle every rule a president issues in the final months of a final term and strike them all down in one vote. It passed the House on a near party-line vote but never received a Senate vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries facing end-of-term federal rules — energy, mining, financial, and other regulated companies — gain a fast tool: instead of lobbying to defeat regulations one at a time, they could see many wiped out in a single resolution with no individual debate. Members of Congress who want quick deregulation also gain, since one vote could clear dozens of rules at once. The bill was passed weeks after the 2016 election, when a new Congress was expected to be hostile to the outgoing administration's rules.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Congressional Review Act so that one joint resolution can disapprove multiple rules at once, as long as each rule was submitted to Congress during the final year of a President's term — the so-called 'midnight rules.'
Today each regulation requires its own resolution, its own debate, and its own vote; the en bloc procedure makes bulk repeal dramatically faster and easier to pass.
The House report version (unchanged from introduction) shows the mechanism plainly: the resolving clause lists multiple rules by agency and subject, and 'such rules shall have no force or effect.'

analysis.who_pays: People who rely on those late-term regulations: a single vote could erase worker-safety, consumer, environmental, and financial protections without any individual debate or record of which specific rule was why. Under the Congressional Review Act, a disapproved rule also cannot be reissued in substantially the same form, so the repeal is a one-way door. Democratic members offered amendments to exempt rules supporting employment and workforce programs; all were rejected.

drawbacks.text: A single up-or-down vote could void many unrelated regulations at once — a workplace-safety rule, a clean-air rule, a consumer rule — with no individual debate or accountability for any of them.
Repeal under the Congressional Review Act is permanent for that rule: agencies cannot reissue a disapproved rule in substantially the same form, so erasing a batch is a one-way ratchet.

An amendment offered by Rep. Mark Pocan to exempt any rule that improves employment, retention, and earnings of workers — especially those with significant barriers to employment — failed 181–239, showing the bill's sponsors were unwilling to carve out even worker-support rules.

The bill applies only in a president's final year, and its practical effect depends on who holds the White House and Congress: the same tool that lets one Congress sweep away a prior administration's rules would exist permanently for every future handoff.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For regulated industries and deregulation-minded lawmakers the benefit is real and large: bulk repeal of inconvenient rules in one vote instead of dozens. The cost falls on the diffuse public — anyone protected by a late-term rule on safety, wages, air, water, or finance — who loses those protections in a vote that never examines any single rule on its merits. Because CRA repeal cannot be undone by reissuing the rule, the cost is durable. This is a procedural change whose whole point is speed and volume of repeal, and its design offers no safeguard for high-stakes rules.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 240–179 on November 17, 2016, but the Senate committee it was sent to never acted, and the bill died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Darrell Issa introduced the bill on September 9, 2016, and it was referred to the Judiciary and Rules Committees.

The House Judiciary Committee ordered it reported on a 15–5 vote on September 14 and formally reported it on September 21; the Rules Committee was discharged and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar.

During floor action on November 17, amendments from Reps. Conyers, Johnson (GA), and Jackson Lee were voted down, and a unanimous-consent set of amendments from Rep. Connolly failed on a recorded-vote demand.
Rep. Mark Pocan's motion to recommit — an instruction to add an exemption for rules supporting employment and workforce earnings — failed 181–239, with Republicans voting 237–0 against it.
The bill passed the House 240–179: Republicans voted 237–0 for it, Democrats 3–179 against.

The Senate received the bill on November 28, 2016, read it twice, and referred it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which took no action before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on end-of-term federal protections came out ahead: the bill died, so each late-term regulation kept the protection of needing an individual repeal vote. Regulated industries did not get the bulk-erasure tool, though Congress retained its existing authority to strike rules one at a time — which the next Congress went on to use in early 2017.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost perfectly by party: 237 of 246 Republicans voted yes and 0 voted no, while 179 of 188 Democrats voted no and only 3 voted yes.

industries.industry: Energy, mining, and other environmentally regulated industries
industries.note: End-of-term rules commonly cover air, water, and land protections. En bloc disapproval would let Congress void many of them in one vote with no individual debate, and CRA repeal bars reissuing the same rule.
Late-term financial and consumer rules could be swept into a batch resolution; each firm benefits from faster, less-scrutinized repeal than the current one-rule-at-a-time process allows.
The rejected Pocan amendment shows the bill reached rules affecting workers' employment and earnings; employers facing such rules would gain a single-vote path to erase them.
